original_value: Human occupancy counting is crucial for both space utilisation and building energy optimisation. In the current article, we present a semi-supervised domain adaptation method for carbon dioxide - Human Occupancy Counter Plus Plus (DA-HOC++), a robust way to estimate the number of people within one room by using data from a carbon dioxide sensor. In our previous work, the proposed Seasonal Decomposition for Human Occupancy Counting (SD-HOC) model can accurately predict the number of individuals when the training and labelled data are adequately available. DA-HOC++ is able to predict the number of occupants with minimal training data: as little as 1 day’s data. DA-HOC++ accurately predicts indoor human occupancy for five different rooms across different countries using a model trained from a small room and adapted to other rooms. We evaluate DA-HOC++ with two baseline methods: a support vector regression technique and an SD-HOC model. The results demonstrate that DA-HOC++’s performance on average is better by 10.87% in comparison to SVR and 8.65% in comparison to SD-HOC.

result.paraphrase: Human occupancy counting is essential for optimizing both space use and building energy efficiency. In this article, we introduce DA-HOC++, a semi-supervised domain adaptation method for carbon dioxide–based Human Occupancy Counter Plus Plus, which robustly estimates the number of people in a single room from carbon dioxide sensor data. Our earlier Seasonal Decomposition for Human Occupancy Counting (SD-HOC) model can accurately forecast occupant numbers when sufficient training and labeled data are available. DA-HOC++ can estimate occupancy with very little training data, requiring as little as one day of data. Trained on a small room and adapted to other rooms, DA-HOC++ accurately predicts indoor human occupancy in five rooms across different countries. We compare DA-HOC++ against two baselines: a support vector regression method and the SD-HOC model. The results show that, on average, DA-HOC++ performs 10.87% better than SVR and 8.65% better than SD-HOC.
